title: I released an AI-assisted indie game demo on Steam. Here's my experience
author: Zestyclose-Date-8476
selftext:
Late 2023, I started building a game.

I already had a lot of experience with programming and Unity, way before AI, so I knew what I was doing. At least for the most part; the rest I learned during the process, as always.

Since I'm a solo developer, this is a hobby/passion project, and my budget is limited, once AI started appearing as a possibility that could assist me, I embraced it about a year ago.

It mainly helped me with art assets (I can't draw a dot), while I focused on the code and the fun part: game design.

This was around two years after the start of the project. By then, I already had a solid gamplay base

With time, I also started using some Codex to help refine certain aspects and save time.

The whole process went smoothly this past year, and I slowly started promoting the game in different communities and social media.

A few days ago, I released the demo on Steam.

Since the game has a Steam page, I disclosed that I use GenAI for some of the art assets, so now I'm "branded."

Naturally, after releasing the demo, I started promoting the game much more actively here and there, tring to get people to actually play it.

I've had at least one comment on almost every post pointing out that I use AI, as if I had killed someone.

In some communities, the post was even deleted as "low effort" because of the use of AI.

Low effort... after three years.

Besides that, I submitted the game to some festivals and got rejected because of the use of GenAI. I've contacted streamers who replied that they can't show the game because it uses GenAI, and I've had many other similar experiences.

So, you understand where I'm going.

From a marketing perspective, we're treated like evil witches that have to be burned.

Is this a rant? Maybe, in a way.

But it's also an encouraging post, because despite all that, I'm almost at 1k wishlists, which isn't bad. I'm not going to be Balatro, but at least I'm getting somewhere.

Also, BECAUSE AI helped me reach this stage, I'm now hiring an artist to help me with some of the art: capsules, splash screens, UI, and now a lore video.

So I'm pretty sure this artist wouldn't have this work from me if it weren't for AI.

  
That's it. I would like to hear similar experiences and your opinion.

comments.author: zayelion
comments.body:
Im in a similar boat. When I get rejection emails the streamer usually has a fursona style avatar. Some I can goad into explaining their positions or to point me to artist in thier circle they personally know that would be will to work at market prices and in the games choicen style and they can't.

Im coming to the conclusion that these are young outside industry artist. There is the myth of the starving artist, when digital art is very lucrative, slow commission painting is not. Product design is lucrative, permissive art use usually is not. Modern art is usually attached to a brand, has to meet technical specification like dimensions style poly count or reproduce IP exactly with minimal variance. Its not self expression which is what I would classify this group as. Its the type of artist you argue your vision over and end up paying double for a compromise and only 1/10th of your needed assets.

Thats not commercial level artistry. Animation is and they are clamping at the bit for faster methods so they spend more time in the creative key frame time rather than gruely in between animation. Or UX designers trying to optimize to get out to a client on time or keep them by offering revisions that don't compromise vision and do not exhaust them.

11% of AAA disclose AI assets currently. That number is going to grow. The AI bubble is going to burst. When that happens it gets the online dating treatment where it becomes an accepted but kinda suboptimal thing.

comments.author: CountryOk4844
comments.body:
I've been a professional software developer for over 20 years and I can tell you that outside of the gaming industry everybody is using AI all the time. I personally haven't written a single line of code this year, I just prompt, review, and make corrections if needed (but I even do that with prompts instead of editing the code in most cases), and 98% of my coder friends and colleagues work like this. It's not vibe coding, I know what the AI is doing and my sessions are short (typically 5-10 minutes of planning, then 10-20 minutes of coding), so everything is under control, but I'm just giving instructions.

Outside of the gaming industry, employers actually encourage - or even enforce - it to increase productivity. I just don't believe that AAA game studios don't do the same secretly, especially when the release date would need to be postponed otherwise.

comments.author: Puffelpuff
comments.body: I checked all your posts and do not see the hate you describe. Most of the answers in the poster are interested in your game. You also have over 1k wishlists... which is more than most indie games on steam. I can´t see any witchhunt here. The most striking thing i can see is your battle field sprites and camera angle makes me dizzy and the generated assets look low quality. Did you touch them up? fix them to look better? i can´t see that here. Why didn´t you use free license assets to have a general direction of the game? What about music? Thats a lot of work to get right with AI. Took me over 800 generates tracks to finally find one that i like and was fitting for the game but it took a lot of time to get it to loop cleanly. The presentation of a game is the most important part. Without artistic vision, out the spark, no matter what you do, the game will get critiqued. With or without AI. In your case most are offering feedback on the visuals, so update and refine them.

comments.author: emperormarkus
comments.body:
I am in the same boat at the moment getting a game ready for Steam release.

I do agree with some of the posters here that the artwork is often the key. How natural does it look? Does it really fit?

I think if you get beyond that then it comes down to the right audience - kids don’t care about AI - and is the game itself different from the crowd.

Keep going. I actually think soon the AI stigma will pass.

As many other folks here say we are all using AI at work and in our personal lives. It will be the norm for everything soon.
